definition: In computer vision, triangulation refers to the process of determining a point in 3D space given its projections onto two, or more, images.
details: In order to solve this problem it is necessary to know the parameters of the camera projection function from 3D to 2D for the cameras involved, in the simplest case represented by the camera matrices. Triangulation is sometimes also referred to as reconstruction or intersection. The triangulation problem is in principle trivial. Since each point in an image corresponds to a line in 3D space, all points on the line in 3D are projected to the point in the image. If a pair of corresponding points in two, or more images, can be found it must be the case that they are the projection of a common 3D point x. The set of lines generated by the image points must intersect at x (3D point) and the algebraic formulation of the coordinates of x (3D point) can be computed in a variety of ways, as is presented below. In practice, however, the coordinates of image points cannot be measured with arbitrary accuracy. Instead, various types of noise, such as geometric noise from lens distortion or interest point detection error, lead to inaccuracies in the measured image coordinates. explainer.lead: Triangulation in computer vision determines a point in 3D space from its projections onto two or more images. It matters for reconstructing 3D structure from multiple views.

tiers.eli5: If two cameras each see the same dot, you can work out where the dot sits in space by where the sight lines cross.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers need the camera projection parameters, in the simplest case camera matrices, to solve it; each image point corresponds to a line in 3D space. It is also called reconstruction or intersection.
tiers.paperLevel: Given projections of a point onto two or more images and the camera projection functions from 3D to 2D, triangulation recovers the 3D point; each image point corresponds to a line in 3D space, and the problem is in principle trivial when parameters are known.

explainer.example: Two calibrated cameras observe the same point; intersecting the two corresponding 3D lines yields the point's position in space.
